messages.subject: loading sam file takes lot of time
messages.subject_clean: loading sam file takes lot of time
messages.body_plain:
Hi
I am trying to load the .sam files from bismark alignment into methylkit R interface.. the file size is around 20gb.
But calling methylation for each sample takes around 5 to 6 hrs.
Is there any way that it can be made to run faster using multi cores.. ?

# my sample code
library(methylKit)
library(graphics)

# this is a list of example files, ships with the package
file.list=list( "44116.R1.fastq_bismark_bt2_pe.deduplicated.sorted.sam",
                "44117.R1.fastq_bismark_bt2_pe.deduplicated.sorted.sam",
                "44121.R1.fastq_bismark_bt2_pe.deduplicated.sorted.sam",
                "44133.R1.fastq_bismark_bt2_pe.deduplicated.sorted.sam",
                "44135.R1.fastq_bismark_bt2_pe.deduplicated.sorted.sam",
                "44137.R1.fastq_bismark_bt2_pe.deduplicated.sorted.sam")

# read the files to a methylRawList object: myobj
myobj=read.bismark(file.list, sample.id <http://sample.id>=list("44116","44117","44121","44133", "44135", "44137"), assembly="hg19",
         save.folder=getwd(), save.context = c("CpG") , read.context="CpG",
                  nolap=FALSE,mincov=10,minqual=20,phred64=FALSE,treatment=c(0,0,0, 1,1,1))

thank you

messages.subject: Benefits of using logistic regression (replicates)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have been reading about how to deal with replicates when preforming differential analysis. And here is what I am understanding:

No replicates:
It is clear that when no replicates are available, the best we can do is a Fischer's exact test ( or a Chi square test).

Replicates:
- When replicates are available, we can choose to be very stringent (i.e  sensitive to small differences) by pooling replicates to force the Fischer's exact test.
- If replicates are kept separated, my understanding (discussed here https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/methylkit_discussion/regression/methylkit_discussion/eLs44aJdIfU/RiR6bIbOrP8J <https://groups.google.com/forum/#%21searchin/methylkit_discussion/regression/methylkit_discussion/eLs44aJdIfU/RiR6bIbOrP8J> ) is that the counts for Cs (methylated) and Ts (unmethylated) are summed across regions and a logistic regression is performed between treatment and control groups.

If keeping replicates separated is meant to access and account for biological variability, I was wondering if this is what is done using logistic regression. Does it take into account this variability?

If we only sum the count across replicates, doesn't that mimic pooling replicates? if that's the case, what is the benefit of keeping replicates separated and using logistic regression? (as opposed to pooling + Fischer's test)

Any input would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Altuna,

I had a couple questions about a bit of code that you shared via your github.

What is the purpose of equalizing the coordinates? Also, I'm confused at that code.

# end of the + strand genes must be equalized to start pos
end(tss.gr <http://tss.gr>[strand(tss.gr <http://tss.gr>)=="+",])  =start(tss.gr <http://tss.gr>[strand(tss.gr <http://tss.gr>)=="+",])
# startof the - strand genes must be equalized to end pos
start(tss.gr <http://tss.gr>[strand(tss.gr <http://tss.gr>)=="-",])=end(tss.gr <http://tss.gr>[strand(tss.gr <http://tss.gr>)=="-",])

Is this a typo? I assume you meant to say:

end position on "+" strand set to start position on "-", and start on "-" strand is set to end position on "+".

Appreciate any clarification.

Thanks,
Stephen

> Best,
> Altuna
